title: Ink-detection models let contestants in the 2023 Vesuvius Challenge read more than 2,000 characters inside an unopened Herculaneum scroll
summary: Ink-detection models that three contestants built on TimeSformer recovered more than 2,000 characters of Greek text inside a sealed Herculaneum scroll, and a later scan confirmed the reading.
account: On 12 October 2023 the Vesuvius Challenge announced that contestant Luke Farritor, a 21-year-old student, had read ΠΟΡΦΥΡΑϹ (“purple”) inside the unopened Herculaneum scroll PHerc. Paris. 4. He used a machine-learning model trained on the “crackle” pattern of ink visible in X-ray computed tomography scans. On 5 February 2024 the organizers gave the $700,000 grand prize to Youssef Nader, Luke Farritor and Julian Schilliger. Their TimeSformer-based ink-detection models recovered 15 columns and more than 2,000 characters of Greek text. Papyrologists Federica Nicolardi, Richard Janko and Robert Fowler reviewed the passages, which discuss pleasure, food and music and are probably by Philodemus. The University of Kentucky, whose virtual-unwrapping software underlies the contest, called the result a new, readable Herculaneum text. On 5 February 2025 the Bodleian Libraries reported that machine-learning ink detection had revealed columns of text in another scroll, PHerc. 172. On 25 June 2026 the Vesuvius Challenge team announced that it had read all surviving text of a further scroll, PHerc. 1667. In that announcement and in a preprint posted on 27 June 2026, the team reported that a new high-resolution scan of PHerc. Paris. 4 shows the ink directly and that this ink matches the 2023 reading.
purpose: The contestants built the models to detect ink in X-ray computed tomography scans of carbonized Herculaneum papyri so that people can read the text. The benefit in this case fulfills that purpose.
system: Vesuvius Challenge grand-prize ink-detection models (TimeSformer-based ensemble) applied to virtually unwrapped CT segments
model_version: 2023 grand-prize submission (TimeSformer-based architecture combined with multiple model architectures)
developer: Youssef Nader, Luke Farritor and Julian Schilliger (contestants)
deployer: Vesuvius Challenge (co-founded by Brent Seales, University of Kentucky)

ratings.reason: Nader, Farritor and Schilliger shared a $700,000 prize announced by the organizers on 5 February 2024. Farritor had earlier won the First Letters prize for the first word.
The readable text validated the University of Kentucky program behind the virtual unwrapping, which Seales described as a 20-year dream.
A previously unknown Greek philosophical text became readable. Nature reports that the method paves the way to deciphering the rest of the scrolls.

ai_role.statement: The contestants' ink-detection models produced the ink images from which papyrologists read the text. The ink is not visible in the raw CT data. Virtual unwrapping (non-AI) was a necessary precondition. The readings were validated by an independent papyrological review organized by the contest.

fields.summary: Ink-detection models that three contestants built on TimeSformer recovered more than 2,000 characters of Greek text inside a sealed Herculaneum scroll, and a later scan confirmed the reading.
fields.account: On 12 October 2023 the Vesuvius Challenge announced that contestant Luke Farritor, a 21-year-old student, had read ΠΟΡΦΥΡΑϹ (“purple”) inside the unopened Herculaneum scroll PHerc. Paris. 4. He used a machine-learning model trained on the “crackle” pattern of ink visible in X-ray computed tomography scans. On 5 February 2024 the organizers gave the $700,000 grand prize to Youssef Nader, Luke Farritor and Julian Schilliger. Their TimeSformer-based ink-detection models recovered 15 columns and more than 2,000 characters of Greek text. Papyrologists Federica Nicolardi, Richard Janko and Robert Fowler reviewed the passages, which discuss pleasure, food and music and are probably by Philodemus. The University of Kentucky, whose virtual-unwrapping software underlies the contest, called the result a new, readable Herculaneum text. On 5 February 2025 the Bodleian Libraries reported that machine-learning ink detection had revealed columns of text in another scroll, PHerc. 172. On 25 June 2026 the Vesuvius Challenge team announced that it had read all surviving text of a further scroll, PHerc. 1667. In that announcement and in a preprint posted on 27 June 2026, the team reported that a new high-resolution scan of PHerc. Paris. 4 shows the ink directly and that this ink matches the 2023 reading.
